For a tail going backward along -Z instead, using the default frame computation without an explicit up vector, the cross product works out to N=(0,-1,0), meaning the local +Z axis leans downward -- so for a tail extending straight back, the normal ends up pointing down rather than up.

For paints, I'll lean on world-space position-based functions since they're robust, like countershading the back versus belly using the surface normal's y-component, plus custom paint functions for specific markings. Now I'm sketching the overall body design for the red panda in a bold, chunky "puppet-of-primitives" style.

For the body, legs, and head, I'm figuring out whether to loft shapes along the spine or just attach primitive geometries like spheres to bones, since simple three.js geometry works fine for pieces like the head, as long as I assign it to the right bone with proper scale and placement. For painting these parts, I'm relying on the fact that paints key off world position and normal rather than needing special UV handling, so even a sphere-based head can take a custom paint function.

Since paint is baked in bind-pose model-space coordinates, I'm realizing I can define facial markings like tear streaks and white cheeks directly as functions of position relative to the head's center, which is the cleanest approach. I'm also working out the texel density needed for the paint sheet based on total surface area of a red panda (roughly 0.6 m²), checking whether a 1024 or 2048 texel sheet gives sufficient resolution — landing around 1-2mm per texel depending on sheet size.

I'm now weighing a tradeoff: higher resolution (2048) gives crisper markings but means baking millions of texel evaluations with noise functions, which could take several seconds; dropping to 1024 cuts that cost roughly fourfold and might be the safer choice given unknown time constraints, even though quality is the priority.

Deciding to go with 1024 and keep paint functions cheap, since even at that resolution the texel density is plenty for fine detail at head scale. I'll paint only the fur-colored meshes (body, head, tail, legs) with the shared texture material, while small flat-colored parts like eyes, nose, and claws use simple per-color materials capped at 64 colors, keeping total painted area around 0.5 m².

For tufts, rather than risky SVG card textures that could render invisible under Node, I'll go with robust low-poly spike geometry instead -- flattened cones for cheek ruffs and small spikes for ear tufts. Now sketching out red panda proportions: head-body length around 56cm, tail about 47cm, shoulder height 25cm standing, 5kg weight, stocky short legs with a slightly arched back.

Working out exact coordinates now -- ground at y=0, feet planted there, body center around y=0.20 with belly at 0.11 and back at 0.29, legs spanning roughly 0.17 down to the ground, and body torso running from hip to chest for about 0.37m length.

Mapping out the spine chain forward from the hips through the chest to the neck and head, giving the back a gentle arch typical of a red panda's posture rather than a flat line. Still refining spine coordinates...
